 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center"><B>SUMMARY OF THE MATERIAL RISKS ASSOCIATED WITH OUR BUSINESS </B></P>
<P STYLE="font-size:12pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="1%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="2%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">We are a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company with a very limited operating history. We have incurred net
losses since our inception and anticipate that we will continue to incur substantial and increasing net losses in the foreseeable future. We may never achieve or sustain profitability. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">A pandemic, epidemic, or outbreak of an infectious disease, such as the global novel coronavirus disease 2019 <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">(&#147;COVID-19&#148;)</FONT> pandemic, may materially and adversely affect our business, including our preclinical studies, clinical trials, third-parties on whom we rely, our supply chain, our ability to raise capital,
and our financial results. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>

capital when needed on acceptable terms, or at all, could force us to delay, limit, reduce or terminate our research, product development or commercialization efforts. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>PART 1 </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>All brand names or trademarks appearing in this report are the property of their respective owners. Unless the context requires otherwise, references in
this report to &#147;Checkmate,&#148; the &#147;Company,&#148; &#147;we,&#148; &#147;us&#148; and &#147;our&#148; refer to Checkmate Pharmaceuticals, Inc. and its subsidiary. </I></P>
<P STYLE="font-size:18pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="9%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left"><B><A NAME="tx18214_1"></A>Item&nbsp;1.</B></TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman; " ALIGN="left"><B>Business. </B></P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Overview </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We are a clinical-stage biotechnology company
focused on developing and commercializing our proprietary technology to harness the power of the immune system to combat cancer. Our product candidate, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001,</FONT> is an advanced generation Toll-like receptor 9
(&#147;TLR9&#148;) agonist delivered as a biologic virus-like particle (&#147;VLP&#148;) utilizing a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT> oligonucleotide as a key component. When injected into a tumor,
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> is designed to trigger the body&#146;s innate immune system, thereby altering the tumor microenvironment and directing activated anti-tumor T cells to attack both the injected tumor and also tumors
throughout the body. In a clinical trial of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with a systemic checkpoint inhibitor (&#147;CPI&#148;) in patients with melanoma whose tumors were unresponsive or no longer responsive to a
CPI, we have observed a best objective response rate (&#147;ORR&#148;) of 28% (27/98), including post-progression responders. We have assembled a strong management team and infrastructure to evaluate <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT>
across multiple tumor types in combination with other immunotherapy agents. Our founder, Art Krieg, first reported the discovery of immunostimulatory cytosine-phosphate-guanine(&#147;CpG&#148;) DNA in 1995, which, combined with the discovery of
TLR9, led to the recognition that synthetic <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT> oligonucleotides have the ability to stimulate the TLR9 receptor for therapeutic purposes. Our goal is to establish
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> as a foundational immuno-oncology therapy that engages the innate immune system to fight cancer and improve outcomes for patients with a broad range of solid tumors. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Many tumors possess mechanisms to evade the immune system. One such evasion mechanism is through the expression of signaling molecules known as immune
checkpoint proteins, which inhibit some immune cells that are capable of mounting an immune response against the tumor. Checkpoint inhibitors, such as antibodies that block programmed death receptor 1 (&#147;
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1&#148;)</FONT> have the ability to reverse this mechanism of evasion, thereby unleashing anti-tumor T cells to destroy tumors. However, except with respect to certain rare tumor types, these therapies are only
effective in a minority of patients, as many patients do not have an activated T cell response targeting their tumors. We have observed increased anti-tumor T cell activity in preclinical and clinical studies of the combination of a CPI with an
innate immune activator of Type I interferons <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">(&#147;IFN-&#945;&#148;)</FONT> a large subgroup of interferon proteins that help regulate the immune system. Of the many different
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">IFN-&#945;</FONT> inducers that have been tested in human immune cells, TLR9 agonist <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT> oligonucleotides have been found to be the most potent in inducing <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">IFN-&#945;.</FONT> We believe that the distinct mechanism of action of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001,</FONT> along with its structure as a VLP, leads to the activation of innate immunity in a way that initiates
or restores a systemic adaptive immune response with anti-tumor T cells. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our top priorities are to (1)&nbsp;Advance the clinical development of <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> toward marketing authorizations for the treatment of melanoma, and (2)&nbsp;Develop <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> for use across other relevant tumor types and indications. We are
conducting a<B> </B>Phase 2 trial of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with nivolumab in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> refractory melanoma. We believe that data
from this trial, if successful, could help support submission of a biologics license application (&#147;BLA&#148;). Additionally, we are conducting a randomized Phase 2 trial of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with
nivolumab in first-line melanoma. In addition to these studies in melanoma, we are conducting a study of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with pembrolizumab in relapsed / refractory metastatic head and neck squamous
cell carcinoma (&#147;HNSCC&#148;) and actively exploring potential trials in other tumor types. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our Phase 1b clinical study has evaluated <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in subjects with advanced <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> refractory melanoma in combination with pembrolizumab and as a monotherapy. In this study,
as of September&nbsp;30, 2020, we observed a best ORR of 28% (27/98), including post-progression responders, when <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> was combined with pembrolizumab. Treatment related adverse events were generally
manageable, the most common consisting of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">flu-like</FONT> symptoms and injection site reactions. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">6 </P>

</DIV></Center>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We are also supporting an investigator-sponsored Phase 2 trial with
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with nivolumab in the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">pre-surgery,</FONT> or neoadjuvant, setting in patients with resectable melanoma not previously treated with <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. Data presented at The Society for the Immunotherapy of Cancer (SITC) on November&nbsp;11, 2020 showed a Pathological Response (pCR, pMR, and pPR) of 70%, a pathological Complete Response
(&#147;pCR&#148;) rate of 50%, and a Major Pathological Response (&#147;MPR&#148;) (pCR and pMR), rate of 60%. We believe these pathological response rates in the neoadjuvant setting support the development of
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in other <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> na&iuml;ve melanoma indications, such as first-line melanoma, which we are pursuing in a clinical
trial. Historical response rates of other TLR9 agonists in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> antibodies in the
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> na&iuml;ve metastatic or unresectable melanoma setting have shown objective response rates ranging from 49 to 76% as compared to an average of only 34 to 40%
with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> therapy alone. We expect that we will be required to conduct a randomized trial comparing <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade versus <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade alone if we pursue marketing authorization in the future in neoadjuvant melanoma. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (&#147;
FDA&#148;) has granted <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001as</FONT> a TLR9 agonist Orphan Drug Designation for the treatment of Stages <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">IIb-IV</FONT> melanoma and Fast Track designation for unresectable Stage III
or Stage IV melanoma and unresectable or metastatic melanoma refractory to prior <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> blockaded. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">To date, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> has been studied in more than 250 melanoma patients in clinical trials. Based on the clinical data we
have generated to date, including the generally manageable adverse events we have observed, we believe there is an opportunity for <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> to be developed as a differentiated immuno-oncology therapy. On the
strength of the clinical results observed in multiple settings of melanoma, we intend to conduct additional trials with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> antibodies. The following table sets forth the current status of our existing trials and our key clinical trials evaluating <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in melanoma as well as our
expansion into new indications with our trial in HNSCC. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Clinical Pipeline </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="font-size:12pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="font-size:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">


<IMG SRC="g18214g13h23.jpg" ALT="LOGO">
 </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We believe that our novel mechanism of action creates significant potential to synergize with CPIs in two unique ways: (1)
through the Type A class of CpG molecule, and (2) through the immunostimulatory effects of the VLP. To our knowledge, CMP-001 is the only investigational CpG-A class TLR9 agonist in clinical trials, and we believe the CpG-A class differs from other
CpG classes in clinical development in their ability induce high levels of IFN-&#945;. CpG-A oligonucleotides contain a native phosphodiester DNA backbone that is cleaved during TLR9 activation in order to generate the strongest possible IFN-&#945;
production. In contrast, CpG-B and CpG-C oligonucleotides, used in other TLR9 clinical studies, consist of TLR9 agonists constructed with a phosphorothioate backbone that cannot be cleaved during plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC) activation, and
therefore induce a lower level of IFN-&#945; production. We believe the differences in molecular structure have a meaningful impact on molecular signaling, and potentially on clinical efficacy. CpG-A activates TLR9 in early endosomes, which is in
turn associated with high IFN-&#945; production. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">7 </P>

</DIV></Center>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our VLP technology is designed to encapsulate and protect the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT>
oligonucleotide from degradation in the tumor. The first injection of the VLP stimulates the production of antibodies to the VLP. On subsequent injections, the antibodies may then bind to the VLP, potentially promoting the uptake of the <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT> cargo into the pDCs via an activating receptor on the pDCs, FcgRIIA, which has been shown in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">pre-clinical</FONT> models to enhance the systemic anti-cancer immune effect. In
contrast, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-B</FONT> and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-C</FONT> oligonucleotides are taken up via oligonucleotide receptors without this added immune effect from the FcgRIIA. We believe this is another
important differentiating factor in the efficacy of our approach. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We believe our VLP technology confers unique properties that<B> </B>enhance therapeutic
immune stimulation. We plan to explore the applicability of our VLP technology as we pursue other innate immune targets beyond TLR9. In addition to our internal drug discovery and development efforts, we plan to explore potential strategic
collaborative relationships, partnerships, acquisitions and licensing opportunities to enhance the development of our current programs and access additional novel product candidates. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">To support our business efforts, we have assembled a management team with extensive experience in pharmaceutical and biologic discovery, development and
commercialization at leading biopharmaceutical and biotechnology companies including Biogen, Coley, Human Genome Sciences, Eli Lilly, Novartis, Pfizer, Takeda, Moderna and Amgen. Since our inception in 2015, through venture funding and our IPO in
August 2020, we have raised $241.7&nbsp;million. Our private rounds included prominent biotechnology institutional investors including Sofinnova Investments, venBio Partners, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">F-Prime</FONT> Capital, Decheng Capital,
Longitude Capital, Novo Holdings, Medixci, Omega Funds, Clough Capital Partners, Sectoral Asset Management, and BrightEdge, the venture investment fund of the American Cancer Society. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Our <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> Program </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> is based on a novel therapeutic approach that consists of two components: (1)&nbsp;a capsid protein that is
produced by fermentation, and is derived from a QBeta RNA bacteriophage and (2)&nbsp;a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT> DNA oligonucleotide that is manufactured by solid phase synthesis. These two components are combined together under
controlled conditions where they self-assemble to form the VLP. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">To date, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> is the only <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT> oligodeoxynucleotide in clinical development to our knowledge and is differentiated in several important ways from other TLR9 agonists in advanced clinical development, which are
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-C</FONT> oligodeoxynucleotides. We believe these differences have resulted in encouraging and differentiated clinical data. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">First, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT> oligodeoxynucleotides are structurally distinct from <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-C</FONT>
oligodeoxynucleotides, and they induce higher levels of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">IFN-&#945;.</FONT> In contrast, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-C</FONT> oligodeoxynucleotides induced less
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">IFN-&#945;</FONT> and more inflammatory cytokines and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Interleukin-10</FONT> (IL-10), a key immune-suppressive cytokine produced by regulatory
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">T-cells,</FONT> when evaluated in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">pre-clinical</FONT> models. Second, the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT> in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> is packaged
in an immunogenic virus-like particle (VLP). A facilitating antibody response develops to the VLP, which is taken up by the target cells (plasmacytoid dendritic cells, or pDCs) through a specific receptor,
Fc<FONT STYLE="FONT-FAMILY:SYMBOL">&#103;</FONT>RIIA (CD32), that provides an additional positive signal to the pDC. In animal models, delivery via the VLP has enhanced the regression of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-injected,</FONT> distant
tumors. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We believe that the clinical data we have generated with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001,</FONT> both in monotherapy and in combination
with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade, demonstrate compelling <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">proof-of-concept</FONT></FONT> consistent with the distinct molecular structure. In combination with
pembrolizumab in patients with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> refractory melanoma, the ORR was 23% (23/98) by RECIST v1.1, and 28% (27/98) when including post-progression responses. The median duration of response was 19.9 months.
Furthermore, we believe that <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> is the only TLR9 agonist to date to demonstrate compelling evidence of single-agent activity, despite the modest duration of response. Finally, we believe <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> is the only TLR9 agonist to date to demonstrate compelling activity in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade in patients with high-risk, Stage III neoadjuvant melanoma. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">8 </P>

</DIV></Center>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Based upon the totality of the data generated to date, we are developing
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade in melanoma and other tumor types. We believe the combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> antibodies is scientifically sound and, if approved, will be commercially attractive compared to combinations with other immune checkpoint inhibitors such as ipilimumab. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Mechanism of Action of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The human immune system possesses an innate ability to recognize and attack a wide variety of pathogens, including bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, as
well as an ability to continuously surveil for dead, dying and diseased tissue. Like humans, bacteria and some viruses have DNA that encode their genome. Unlike humans, however, the DNA of viruses and bacteria has a distinct molecular structure with
unmethylated CpG DNA which activates dedicated TLR9 receptors in pDCs. CpG DNA are relatively common in bacterial and viral DNA but are suppressed and methylated in human and other vertebrate DNA. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Once in an activated state, pDCs secrete large quantities of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">IFN-&#945;</FONT> to put the innate and adaptive immune system
in a position to fight off infections and foreign bodies, such as tumors. This activation is critical since, in their resting, unactivated state in the microenvironment of many solid tumors, pDCs play an immunoinhibitory role in which they protect
tumors from immune attack. We believe that <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> can reverse this unfavorable pDC phenotype present in many tumors by causing these innate immune cells to trigger the body&#146;s adaptive immune system,
leading to a tumor-specific, T cell response. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> is structurally and biologically distinct from other TLR9
agonists in clinical development. It consists of unmethylated <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT> DNA on a natural phosphodiester backbone and self-aggregates into <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">G-quadruplex</FONT> structures that are
encapsulated in a virus-like particle to make it appear like a virus to pDCs. The graphic below illustrates the hypothetical mechanism of action of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001.</FONT> </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Unactivated pDCs can be recruited into tumors and protect them from immune attack. Injections of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> cause an
antibody response to the VLP, which has been shown in preclinical studies to enhance the uptake of antibody-coated <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> into pDCs through the activating Fc receptor, CD32. These studies also demonstrated
that the VLP enhanced the systemic effect of the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A</FONT> beyond that of unencapsulated <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CpG-A.</FONT> The natural phosphodiester backbone allows the CpG DNA to be cleaved inside
the early endosome of the pDC, and has been shown to mediate greater activation of pDCs through TLR9. Activated pDCs can release large amounts of Type I interferons, which facilitate recruitment and activation of other immune cells, such as
conventional dendritic cells, and T cells. We believe these effects can potentially culminate in the generation of large numbers of tumor-targeted T cells capable of killing the tumor both locally and systemically. </P>
<P STYLE="font-size:12pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="font-size:0pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">


<IMG SRC="g18214g24t21.jpg" ALT="LOGO">

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Our Development Strategy </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Our clinical development strategy for <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> is focused on two key pillars. First, on the strength of our clinical
data to date, we intend to continue advancing clinical development toward a regulatory submission seeking approval of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> for the treatment of advanced melanoma. Second, because we believe that the
mechanism of action for <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and the potential to enhance the effectiveness of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade are not limited to melanoma, we intend to develop <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in other relevant tumor types and indications, with an initial focus on head and neck cancer. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Clinical Data
Supporting Our <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> Development Plan </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We have based our development plan on clinical data from three data
sets: </P> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">

STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> refractory melanoma </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>

<TD WIDTH="5%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">3.</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman; " ALIGN="left">Single-agent <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> treatment in patients with <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> refractory melanoma </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">These data, which are described in further detail below, show that <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> has been generally well-tolerated and has demonstrated preliminary anti-tumor activity in patients in combination with a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade in both <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> refractory melanoma and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> na&iuml;ve, neoadjuvant melanoma settings. While there has not been a
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">head-to-head</FONT></FONT> clinical trial comparing the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> therapy combination with single agent <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> therapy, we believe that the
data generated to date supports further clinical evaluation of this combination. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Melanoma is a particularly dangerous form of cancer because of its
ability to spread to other organs rapidly if not surgically removed at an early stage, as well as low response rates and limited durability of response when treated with commonly used chemotherapeutics. In 2020, melanoma of the skin is estimated to
be the fifth most diagnosed cancer, and accounts for approximately 1% of all skin cancers in the United States. Estimates by the American Cancer Society of new diagnoses and deaths as a result of melanoma in the United States are 100,350 and 6,850
respectively. Most cases of melanoma are diagnosed at an early-stage and can often be cured with surgery alone. Patients diagnosed with early-stage melanoma typically have a five-year survival rate of 99%. More advanced melanoma can result in
widespread metastasis to organs, including the skin, lung, brain, liver or intestines, and is less responsive to systemic therapy. Until the introduction of CPIs, treatment for metastatic melanoma primarily included surgery, radiation therapy,
chemotherapy, interferon, or a combination of these treatments. According to data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (&#147;SEER&#148;) program, the five-year survival rate for metastatic melanoma patients is only approximately
25%. Despite the significant rates of responses achieved with CPIs compared to historical standards of care in patients with metastatic melanoma, a large portion of patients still do not respond to immunotherapy and only about half of all melanomas
have genetic mutations that make them suitable for treatment with targeted therapies. Therefore, additional novel therapies are needed to expand the potential of immunotherapy to more patients. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Based on key opinion leader discussions, we believe a substantial proportion of patients with melanoma have at least one lesion that is accessible for
intratumoral injection. These include cutaneous and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">sub-cutaneous</FONT> lesions as well as palpable lymph nodes. To the extent that injection of a single lesion has been shown to have a systemic (abscopal) effect,
patients with a single accessible lesion may be candidates for treatment with drugs administered by intratumoral injection. In clinical trials with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001,</FONT> injections have often been performed in outpatient
clinics, by physicians, nurse practitioners, and nurses&#151;often without the need for any imaging to assist in the procedure. These injections have been generally described to be similar to subcutaneous injections with various agents. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">10 </P>

</DIV></Center>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Phase 1b Study of Intratumoral <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in Patients with <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> Refractory Melanoma </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In October 2015, we initiated a <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">two-part</FONT> Phase 1b clinical trial to assess the effects of intratumoral <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in adult patients with advanced melanoma. In this trial, treatment with <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with pembrolizumab has been generally well-tolerated, and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> reversed or overcame resistance to <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> therapy in some patients with melanoma that progressed on prior <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> therapy. We believe these data provide the
foundation to pursue further Phase 2 studies with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with an <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> antibody in patients who have
metastatic or unresectable melanoma, particularly those with disease progression despite prior treatment with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><U>Part 1&#151;Combination Treatment with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and Pembrolizumab </U></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Trial Design and Endpoints </I></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In Part 1 of the Phase 1b
study, which is fully enrolled, adult patients with metastatic or unresectable melanoma who did not respond or had disease progression after at least four doses of treatment that included <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade were
eligible for enrollment in the trial. The objectives of the study are to determine the recommended dose and schedule of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> when given in combination with pembrolizumab, or KEYTRUDA, and to assess and
describe the safety profile, pharmacodynamics, and anti-tumor activity of the combination. Clinical benefit is being assessed through measurements of objective tumor response and duration of response every 12 weeks by the site investigators
according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (&#147;RECIST&#148;) v1.1. Patients with progressive disease were allowed to continue study treatment at the discretion of the investigator. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As of September&nbsp;30, 2020, we enrolled 159 patients and assessed five dose levels, two dose schedules, and two formulations of <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> (polysorbate 20 (&#147;PS20&#148;) at 0.01% and 0.00167% concentrations) in Part 1 of this study given intratumorally in combination with pembrolizumab, which was administered intravenously every three weeks
according to the US Prescribing Information. The median age of the patients was 64 years and 56% were male. The median number of prior therapies was two (with a range of one to eight), and all patients received one or more prior regimens containing <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. Seventy-five percent (119/159) of patients received monotherapy <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade and 50% (80/159) received <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade in
combination with other agents. Forty-seven percent of the patients had prior ipilimumab as a single agent and/or in combination with other drugs. The best response to prior therapy that included <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade
was progressive disease (&#147;PD&#148;) in 43% of the patients, stable disease (&#147;SD&#148;) in 31% of the patients, PR in 13% of patients and a complete response, or CR, in 4% of patients and 8% were unknown. Prior to enrollment, the last
response assessment of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blocking antibody therapy was PD in 93% of patients, SD in 3% and unknown in 4%. Sixty-five percent of patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (&#147;ECOG&#148;)
performance status of zero and 35% had an ECOG performance status of one. <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Thirty-six</FONT> percent had melanoma with a BRAF mutation. The lactate dehydrogenase (&#147;LDH&#148;) an adverse prognostic factor in
patients with melanoma, was elevated in 42% of patients at baseline. The baseline disease locations in patients enrolled to the study included skin only in 8% of patients, lymph nodes (with or without skin lesions) in 19%, soft tissue (with or
without skin lesions or lymph node metastases) in 13%, bone (with or without skin, lymph nodes, or soft tissue but without visceral metastases) in 4%, and any visceral metastases in 55%. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Anti-tumor Activity </I></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We believe that we have demonstrated
proof of concept for <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with pembrolizumab in the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> refractory melanoma patient setting based on the results from this trial. In the 98 patients
who initiated treatment with intratumoral <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in 0.01% PS20, which was selected for subsequent development based on the results of this study, we observed that 28% (27/98) of these patients had a partial
or complete response, including patients who responded to continued treatment after initial disease progression. The group of 98 also had a best ORR by RECIST v1.1 of 23% (23/98). The best ORR by RECIST v1.1 in the 61 patients who initiated
treatment with intratumoral <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> 0.00167% PS20 was 11% (7/61). A publication in 2020 from the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">KEYNOTE-002</FONT> study reported that six patients out of 78 (7.7%) achieved
an objective response with continued pembrolizumab treatment after initial disease progression. Based on this report, we believe that a response rate above 7% would be indicative of a treatment effect in excess of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> treatment alone. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">11 </P>

</DIV></Center>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In all the 159 patients who were treated by <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination
with pembrolizumab, the Kaplan-Meier analysis produced a median duration of response of 19.9 months for all 37 responders including post-progression responders, and 19.9 months for the 30 responders with a RECIST v1.1 response as of the cutoff date.
</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We believe that the response rate and durability of response observed with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> treatment in combination with
pembrolizumab in these patients provides strong evidence that <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> administered intratumorally in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade has the potential to address the
unmet medical need for patients with melanoma that is progressing despite administering a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. The activity of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with pembrolizumab was
observed in both injected and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-injected</FONT> target lesions, as shown in the figure below. The magnitude of regression between the injected and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-injected</FONT> lesions was
similar. In these responding patients, the mean regression across all injected target lesions was 71% and the mean regression across all <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-injected</FONT> target lesions was 62%. </P>

September&nbsp;30, 2020, of the 159 patients enrolled in Part 1 of the Phase 1b clinical trial, all but three have experienced at least one adverse event assessed as treatment-related by the investigator. The most common adverse events were Grade 1
or 2 and include <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">flu-like</FONT> symptoms and injection site reactions. Treatment-related adverse events reported in at least 20% of patients included: chills (119 patients, 75%); pyrexia (98 patients, 62%); fatigue

hypotension (32 patients, 20%). Sixteen patients (10%) discontinued treatment due to an adverse event. Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation which were considered related to treatment included pneumonitis (n=2) and atrial fibrillation,
chills, diarrhea, disseminated intravascular dissemination, dyspnea, generalized edema, injection related reaction, injection site pain, muscular weakness, pancreatitis (n=1 each). Twenty-seven patients (17%) experienced a treatment-related serious

bronchitis, cardiac failure congestive, chills, confusional state, deep vein thrombosis, diarrhea, disseminated intravascular coagulation, encephalopathy, eye inflammation, fatigue, generalized edema, intracranial hemorrhage, nausea, peripheral
edema, peripheral ischemia, pneumonitis, tumor pain, vomiting (n=1 patient, 0.6%). Fifty-eight patients (36%) experienced one or more treatment-related adverse events of Grade 3 or higher. The most common Grade 3 or 4 treatment-related

adverse events reported in at least three patients included hypotension (n=11, 7%), hypertension (n=8, 5%), chills, back pain (n=5 each, 3%), increased AST, hypoxia, pyrexia (n=4 each, 2.5%),
anemia, increased ALT, arthralgia, and hypophosphatemia (n=3 each, 2%). </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><U>Part 2&#151;Monotherapy Treatment with
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> </U></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Trial Design and Endpoints </I></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In Part 2 of the Phase 1b clinical trial, which has been fully enrolled, adult patients with metastatic or unresectable melanoma who did not respond or had
disease progression after at least four doses of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade were eligible for treatment. The objectives of Part 2 are to evaluate the safety, tolerability and anti-tumor activity of monotherapy <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001.</FONT> Patients with progressive disease on <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> monotherapy had the option to receive <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with pembrolizumab.
</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Interim Anti-tumor Activity </I></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In an interim analysis
of the ongoing trial as of the data <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">cut-off</FONT> date of September&nbsp;30, 2020, 40 patients were treated with intratumoral <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> at initial doses of 5 mg or 10 mg. The
median age of the patients was 68 years and 65% were male. The median number of prior lines of treatment was two (with a range of one to seven). Lactate dehydrogenase was elevated in 45% of the patients and 30% had a BRAF mutation. The ECOG PS was 0
in 50% and 1 in 50% of the patients. The last response on therapy containing a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blocking antibody was progressive disease in 80% (32 patients), stable disease in 10% (4 patients), partial response in 5% (2
patients), and unknown in 5% (2 patients). The best response on therapy containing a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blocking antibody was progressive disease in 23% (9 patients), stable disease in 45% (18 patients), partial response in
13% (5 patients), complete response in 5% (2 patients), and unknown in 15% (6 patients). Forty-three percent of the patients (17 patients) received prior treatment with ipilimumab as a single agent and/or in combination with other agents. As of the
cutoff date, seven patients achieved a partial response for a best ORR of 18%. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Patients enrolled in Part 2 are allowed to have pembrolizumab added to
their <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> continuing regimen at the time of disease progression. While we believe the early activity observed in patients treated with of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> is encouraging, the
duration of response with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> monotherapy has been less than observed in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. We therefore plan to focus subsequent development of <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combinations that include <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Safety Results </I></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As of September&nbsp;30, 2020, forty patients enrolled and 38 (95%) had at least one treatment-related adverse event. The most common treatment-related adverse
events (reported in at least 20% of patients) to single-agent <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> included chills (21 patients, 53%); nausea (19 patients, 48%); pyrexia (18 patients, 45%); fatigue (15 patients, 38%), headache (14
patients, 35%), hypotension (10 patients, 25%); back pain, decreased appetite, vomiting (9 patients, 23%), and pruritus(8 patients, 20%). </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Nine patients
(23%) experienced one or more treatment-related Grade 3 adverse events, which included hypotension, infusion related reaction (2 patients, 5%), and increased ALT, increased AST, bone pain, bradycardia, flank pain, headache, hypertension, pyrexia,
rash, spinal pain, and syncope (1 patient, 3%). There were no Grade 4 or 5 treatment-related adverse events reported at the time of data <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">cut-off.</FONT> </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Six patients (15%) experienced one or more treatment-related SAEs. SAEs considered related to study treatments included hypotension (3 patients, 8%) and
bradycardia, chills, cytokine release syndrome, dizziness, headache, nausea, pemphigoid, presyncope, rash, and syncope (1 patient, 3%). Three patients discontinued study treatment due to adverse events considered related to study treatment including
one subject who had bradycardia, hypotension, and presyncope, one subject who had an injection site reaction, and one subject who had headache, nausea, chills and rigors. </P>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Trial Design and Treatment Extension </I></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The safety of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> when administered in combination with pembrolizumab or as monotherapy will continue to be
evaluated in the Treatment Extension. Enrollment into the Treatment Extension is available to patients receiving treatment in Part 1 or Part 2 at the discretion of the investigator. Patients will continue their current treatment regimen with reduced
study assessments focused on the collection of safety data. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Investigator-sponsored Clinical Trial of
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in Combination with Nivolumab in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> Na&iuml;ve Neoadjuvant Melanoma Patient Setting </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We are currently supporting an investigator-sponsored clinical trial in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> na&iuml;ve neoadjuvant melanoma. In August
2018, investigators at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center began a trial to evaluate <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with nivolumab as neoadjuvant therapy in patients with resectable melanoma not previously
treated with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. Data from this trial, as described below, have shown that <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with nivolumab has been generally well-tolerated and has not
delayed or complicated surgery. We believe the high pathological response rate, including pCR and MPR rates, observed in this investigator-sponsored trial, combined with the generally manageable adverse events we have observed in our clinical trials
of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001,</FONT> provide supporting evidence for the potential of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade in patients with melanoma
na&iuml;ve to <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade in both the neoadjuvant and first-line settings. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Trial Design and Endpoints
</I></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Eligible patients had resectable Stage IIIB, IIIC, or IIID melanoma and had never received treatment that included
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. The trial enrolled 31 patients of which all patients were evaluable for safety and 30 patients were evaluable for the primary endpoint. The trial design consisted of weekly doses of <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> for seven consecutive weeks in combination with three doses of nivolumab at <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">two-week</FONT> intervals. Patients undergo surgical resection and recovery between weeks eight
and 10, after which they will receive adjuvant nivolumab in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> administered local regionally and draining of lymph nodes for up to 54 weeks. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The primary endpoint of this trial was to evaluate MPR in patients with stage IIIB/C melanoma following 7 weeks of nivolumab and injected <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001.</FONT> The secondary objectives were to evaluate safety, relapse-free survival (RFS), and overall survival (OS) after 52 weeks of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">nivolumab/CMP-001</FONT> combination. Final data
on the primary endpoint from this ongoing trial were presented on November&nbsp;11, 2020 at the 35th Annual Meeting of The Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer and are described below. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Final Anti-Tumor Activity </I></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As of the <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">cut-off</FONT> date of October&nbsp;1, 2020, 31 patients were enrolled in the trial, and 30 completed neoadjuvant treatment and surgery and were evaluable for the primary endpoint. One patient experienced systemic
progression prior to surgery and was evaluable for safety but not for pathological response. Patients had a median age of 61 years (with a range from ages <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">19-93),</FONT> and 16 male and 14 female patients were
included in the efficacy analysis for pathological response. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Pathologic Response rate was 70%, including pCR of 50% (15/30), pMR of 10% (3/30), and
pPR of 10% (3/30). The MPR (pCR and pMR) rate was 60%, and 9 patients (30%) did not have a pathological response (pNR). The landmark <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">1-year</FONT> RFS was 90% in patients with a pathological response and 89% in
patients with a MPR. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Biopsies from patients with a pathological response to <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with nivolumab
showed increased density of intratumoral cluster of differentiation 8 (&#147;CD8+&#148;) and T cells and immunophenotyping studies revealed an increased fraction of circulating CD8+Ki67+ T cells in the blood, suggesting that treatment with <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and nivolumab was able to activate CD8+ T cells and facilitate T cell infiltration of the tumor </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">14 </P>

</DIV></Center>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">
microenvironment. Additional studies demonstrated a rim of CD303+ pDCs surrounding <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-viable</FONT> tumor in biopsies from some patients. We believe this is
important, as tumors that exclude T cells are less likely to respond to immunotherapy with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade, and the potential involvement of pDCs supports our proposed mechanism of action for <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001.</FONT> </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Interim Safety Results </I></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The treatment with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and nivolumab was observed to be generally well-tolerated and most treatment related adverse
events were Grade 1 or 2, including <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">flu-like</FONT> symptoms and injection site reactions. The incidence of immune-related adverse events was low, and one patient had Grade 3 colitis. No dose limiting toxicities were
observed, and the most frequent Grade 3 toxicity was hypertension, which was reversible in all cases. No Grade 4 or 5 treatment related adverse events were observed. One patient with a Grade 4 skin infection (not related to <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and nivolumab) had a delay in surgery although disease remained resectable. There were no delays in planned surgery due to treatment related adverse events. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Third-Party Neoadjuvant Clinical Trial Data </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In a
randomized, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-comparative</FONT> trial of four doses of nivolumab at <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">two-week</FONT> intervals in 12 patients and nivolumab plus ipilimumab at three week intervals in 11 patients
conducted at MD Anderson Cancer Center, nivolumab yielded a pCR rate of 25% and ORR of 25% as measured by RECIST v.1.1, while nivolumab plus ipilimumab resulted in a pCR rate of 45% and ORR of 73%. This trial was stopped early due to the inferior
outcomes with nivolumab monotherapy and the high rate of Grade 3 or higher adverse events (75%) with the combination. In the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">OpACIN-neo</FONT> trial conducted by the Netherlands Cancer Institute, 86 patients were
randomized and treated in one of three cohorts of nivolumab and combined with ipilimumab at varying doses and schedules. The objective response rate ranged from 35% to 63%, and the pCR rate ranged from 23% to 57% across the cohorts. The rate of
Grade 3 or higher adverse events ranged from 20 to 50%, and one of the three cohorts was closed by the Data Safety Monitoring Board for toxicity. The PRADO Trial, which was an extension of the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">OpACIN-neo</FONT>
trial, reported a pCR rate of 50% and an MPR rate of 61% from 99 patients treated with two doses of neoadjuvant ipilimumab (1 mg/kg) and nivolumab (3 mg/kg) at a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">3-week</FONT> interval prior to surgery. <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Twenty-two</FONT> percent of the patients experienced a treatment-related Grade 3 or higher immune-related adverse event. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Phase 1b Trial of Subcutaneous <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> In Patients with Advanced Melanoma </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Trial Design and Endpoints </I></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In January 2017, we initiated
a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">two-part</FONT> clinical trial of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> administered subcutaneously in combination with pembrolizumab in patients with advanced melanoma to evaluate whether subcutaneous <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> is a viable route of treatment in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. This trial was undertaken to evaluate whether subcutaneous injection near the tumor or in the
tumor-draining lymph node bed is able to generate a T cell-specific anti-tumor immune response. To be eligible for this trial, patients are required to have metastatic or unresectable melanoma and have continued disease progression despite at least
four doses of treatment that included <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. The objectives of the trial are to determine the recommended Phase 2 dose of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> when administered
subcutaneously in combination with pembrolizumab, and to assess and describe the safety profile, pharmacodynamics, and anti-tumor activity of the combination. <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> was to be injected into an area
corresponding to the lymphatic drainage for one or more melanoma lesions. Clinical benefit was assessed through measurements of objective tumor response and duration of response every 12 weeks by the site investigators according to RECIST v1.1.
Patients with progressive disease are allowed to continue study treatment at the discretion of the investigator. </P>

 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Trial Status </I></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As of a cutoff date of June&nbsp;1, 2020, in the Part 1 dose-escalation phase of the trial, 27 patients were administered

<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Interim Anti-tumor Activity </I></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As of the cutoff date, 25

with a RECIST v1.1 best response of stable disease, eleven (42%) patients with a RECIST v1.1 best response of progressive disease, and four (16%) patients who discontinued prior to having a post baseline tumor assessment. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Interim Safety Results </I></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As of the cutoff date, in the
Part 1 dose-escalation phase of the trial, 27 patients received <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> SC. All but four patients had at least one adverse event assessed as treatment-related by the Investigator. Most were Grade 1 or 2
adverse events, and included <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">flu-like</FONT> symptoms and injection site reactions. Four patients (15%) had one or more treatment-related adverse events of Grade 3 or higher which included increased LDH, erythema
multiforme, fatigue, pain and tumor pain (1 patient, 4%). One patient (4%) discontinued treatment due to an adverse event of pain due to disease progression that was unrelated to study treatment. Two patients (8%) had a treatment-related serious
adverse event. One patient had Grade 3 tumor pain in the abdomen and one had Grade 3 erythema multiforme. Adverse events considered related to study treatment occurring in at least 20% of patients included fatigue (14 patients, 52%); chills (6
patients, 22%), and nausea (6 patients, 22%). </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Clinical Development Plans </B></P>

 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Collaboration with BMS </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">On December&nbsp;7, 2020, we entered into a clinical collaboration with Bristol-Myers Squibb Company (&#147;BMS&#148;), pursuant to which BMS agreed to provide
nivolumab for our Phase 2 refractory melanoma study and Phase 2 first-line melanoma study, at its own expense. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Phase 2 Clinical Trial in <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> Refractory Melanoma </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We are conducting Trial <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001-010,</FONT></FONT> a multicenter, open-label, Phase 2 trial of intratumoral <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with intravenous nivolumab in patients
with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> refractory melanoma. We plan to conduct this trial at clinical sites in the United States. The primary outcome measure is to determine the confirmed
objective response (ORR) based on RECIST v1.1 as assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR). The secondary outcome measures include safety and tolerability, duration of response (DOR), treatment response in
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-injected</FONT> target lesions, progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), immune objective response rate (iORR), immune duration of response (iDOR), immune progression-free survival (iPFS),
pharmacokinetics, and immunogenicity. Trial sites have been activated and patient screening is underway. Approximately 100 patients are planned to be enrolled. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Randomized Phase 2/3 Clinical Trial in First-line Melanoma </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We are conducting Trial <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001-011,</FONT></FONT> a multi-center, Phase 2/3 randomized,
active-controlled, open-label trial of intratumoral <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with intravenous nivolumab versus nivolumab alone in patients with previously untreated advanced or metastatic melanoma. The primary
outcome measure for Phase 2 is to determine the confirmed ORR of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with nivolumab versus nivolumab monotherapy based on RECIST v1.1 as determined by BICR. The secondary outcome measures
for Phase 2 include safety and tolerability. A total of 140 patients will be enrolled in Phase 2, and if the primary endpoint of Phase 2 is met, the trial may proceed into Phase 3 with a total trial sample size of approximately 450&nbsp;patients.
The primary outcome measure for Phase 3 is to evaluate the PFS of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with nivolumab versus nivolumab monotherapy based on RECIST v1.1 as determined by BICR. The secondary outcome measures
for 3 include safety and tolerability, OS; confirmed ORR, DOR, and disease control rate (DCR) based on RECIST v1.1 as determined by BICR; treatment response in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-injected</FONT> target lesions, iPFS, iDOR, and
iORR. In March 2021, we initiated patient dosing in the trial. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We believe that these two trials will inform and enable a registration strategy in <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> na&iuml;ve first-line melanoma, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> refractory melanoma, or both, including a potential Phase 3 registrational trial in first-line melanoma. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Regulatory Status of Melanoma Development Program </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In
February 2020, we received Orphan Drug Designation for a TRL9 agonist <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">(CMP-001)</FONT> for the treatment of Stages <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">IIb-IV</FONT> melanoma. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In March 2020, we met with the FDA to discuss the potential for pursuing accelerated approval of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> based upon
the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">single-arm</FONT> trial in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> refractory melanoma described above, and to pursue full approval in <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CPI-na&iuml;ve</FONT> first-line melanoma based upon a randomized trial comparing <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade vs. <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade alone. With respect to our plans to seek accelerated approval in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT> refractory melanoma, the FDA indicated that we
would likely be required to provide ORR data from a randomized trial to assess the contribution of individual components to the effect of the combination. In July 2020, we received Fast Track designation for
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> for unresectable Stage III or Stage IV melanoma and unresectable or metastatic melanoma refractory to prior <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD-1</FONT></FONT>
blockade. We plan to generate ORR data from the planned randomized first-line melanoma trial described above, but there is no guarantee that such ORR data will support a BLA seeking accelerated approval of
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">anti-PD1</FONT> refractory melanoma. </P>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We intend to seek data exclusivity or market exclusivity for our product candidates provided under the
Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act (&#147;FDCA&#148;) and similar laws in other countries. We believe that <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> could qualify for 12 years of data exclusivity, from the date of approval, under the
Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act of 2009 (&#147;BPCIA&#148;), which was enacted as part of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act. Under the BPCIA, a BLA cannot be submitted to the FDA until four years, or if approved by the
FDA, until 12 years, after the original brand product identified as the reference product is approved under a BLA. The BPCIA provides an abbreviated pathway for the approval of biosimilar and interchangeable biological products. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>II. Develop <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> For Use Across Other Tumor Types and Indications </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We believe <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> has the potential to be developed for any cancer type where
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade has shown some degree of efficacy, but where significant unmet medical need remains. We are conducting a clinical trial in HNSCC in patients who have not yet received treatment with <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. We are also collaborating with an affiliate of Merck KGaA (&#147;Merck&#148;) and Pfizer, Inc. (&#147;Pfizer&#148;), and supporting a small number of investigator-sponsored studies in melanoma and
other cancers. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">HNSCC represents a number of different malignant tumors that develop in or around the throat, larynx, nose, sinuses and mouth, and
accounts for approximately 3.6% of all cancers in the United States. Most head and neck cancers are squamous cell carcinomas. According to the American Cancer Society, there will be an estimated 53,260 new diagnoses and approximately 10,750 patients
will die as a result of head and neck cancer in the United States in 2020. HNSCC is more than twice as prevalent among men, and most cases are believed to be related to tobacco or alcohol use. The human papilloma virus is an important and common
cause of head and neck cancer, particularly in younger patients. According to the American Cancer Society, the five-year survival rate for HNSCC is approximately 65%. Treatments for HNSCC include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted
therapy, or a combination of treatments. HNSCC tumors are an attractive setting for immunotherapy clinical research as they have a high tumor mutation burden leading to the expression of a number of tumor-specific antigens that could lead to
recognition by the adaptive immune system and killing of the tumor by tumor-specific T cells. While nivolumab was approved for treatment of patients with recurrent and metastatic HNSCC with ORR of 13.3% and pembrolizumab was approved for first-line
treatment of HNSCC with ORR of 19%, based on the ORR for these agents, we believe there is a significant unmet clinical need for new treatment options. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and Pembrolizumab in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> Na&iuml;ve HNSCC </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We are conducting a Phase 2 trial of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and pembrolizumab in approximately 43 patients with HNSCC that have not
been previously treated with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> blockade. Eligible patients for this trial are expected to have recurrent or metastatic cancers of the oropharynx, oral cavity, hypopharynx, or larynx that are incurable with
available therapies. Treatment is expected to include intratumoral injections of <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> combined with pembrolizumab at its approved dose and schedule. The primary outcome measure is to determine the
confirmed, investigator-assessed ORR based on RECIST v1.1. The secondary outcome measures include safety and tolerability; efficacy characterized by DOR, PFS, OS, iORR, iDOR, and iPFS; and the effect of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and
programmed death ligand 1 <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">(PD-L1)</FONT> expression on efficacy.&nbsp;Trial sites have been activated and patient screening is underway. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and Avelumab in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PD-1</FONT> Refractory HNSCC </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Collaboration with Merck KGaA and Pfizer </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In September
2018, we entered into a clinical collaboration with Merck and Pfizer in the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Pfizer-sponsored</FONT> JAVELIN Medley Trial. Combination F in the JAVELIN Medley Trial evaluates the safety and efficacy of three cohorts:
(1)&nbsp;avelumab in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001;</FONT> (2) avelumab in combination with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and utomilumab, and (3)&nbsp;avelumab in combination with <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">PF-04518600</FONT> in patients with advanced </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">18 </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As of November&nbsp;15, 2020, the identified risks associated with <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> administration in three Checkmate-sponsored

of the trial are safety, response in the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-injected,</FONT> <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-irradiated</FONT> lesions and PFS. To date, no data have been publicly disclosed by Sheba Medical Center. </P>

rate of treatment with intratumoral <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> combined with intravenous pembrolizumab. To date, no data have been publicly disclosed by the University of Iowa. </P>

in the future. Our competitors include </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The term of individual patents depends upon the legal patent term in the countries in which they are obtained. In most countries in which we file, the patent

may also be eligible for a patent term extension, which permits restoration of a portion of the patent term elapsed during the U.S. clinical development and FDA regulatory review process. The Hatch-Waxman Act permits a patent term extension of up to
five years beyond the expiration of the patent. The length of the patent term extension is related to the length of time the drug is under clinical development in the United States and the length of time the drug is under regulatory review. Patent
term extension cannot extend the remaining term of a patent beyond a total of 14 years from the date of product approval and only one patent applicable to an approved drug may be extended. Similar provisions are available in Europe and other foreign
jurisdictions to extend the term of a patent that covers an approved drug. In the future, if and when our products receive FDA approval, and if and when patents are granted, we expect to apply for patent term extensions on patents covering those
products. We plan to seek patent term extensions for each of our issued patents in any jurisdiction where these are available, however there is no guarantee that the applicable authorities, including the FDA in the United States, will agree with our
assessment of whether such extensions should be granted, and if granted, the length of such extensions. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We may rely, in some circumstances, on trade

(&#147;BPCIA&#148;), which was enacted as part of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act. Under the BPCIA, a BLA cannot be submitted to the FDA until four years, or if approved by the FDA, until 12 years, after the original brand product
identified as the reference product is approved under a BLA. The BPCIA provides an abbreviated pathway for the approval of biosimilar and interchangeable biological products. </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We do not have any manufacturing facilities or personnel. We currently rely, and expect to continue to rely, on third parties for the manufacture of <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">CMP-001</FONT> and any future product candidates for preclinical and clinical testing, as well as for commercial manufacture if our product candidates receive marketing approval. We source our manufacturing and supply
requirements with a number of contract manufacturing organizations (&#147;CMOs&#148;) through the issuance of work orders on an <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">as-needed</FONT> basis. We currently do not have any long-term supply contracts. We
depend and will continue to depend on our CMOs to manufacture our drug candidates in accordance with current Good Manufacturing Practices (&#147;cGMP&#148;) regulations for use in clinical trials. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">We manage multiple CMOs to develop and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">manufacture&nbsp;CMP-001&nbsp;drug</FONT>
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">product.&nbsp;CMP-001&nbsp;is</FONT> a VLP comprised of a Qb (&#147;Qbeta&#148;) coat protein that is assembled around an
<FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">immunostimulatory&nbsp;CpG-A&nbsp;oligodeoxynucleotide,</FONT> G10. Qb is recombinantly produced by fermentation in E. coli, and then purified free of other cellular material at one of our CMOs. The G10
oligonucleotide is produced via solid support phosphoramidite chemistry at one of two additional CMOs. The two drug substance intermediates, Qb and G10, are combined in an aqueous salt buffer where they self-assemble into virus-like particles prior
to final purification of the drug substance at another CMO. Another CMO performs the fill and finish of the final drug product. </P>
